title: Virtual Medical Receptionist: Human vs AI Cost Compared
summary: A human virtual medical receptionist costs $3.45–$5.00 per call minute. AI costs $0.07–$1.00. Here is what that gap buys, and where it does not.
body_markdown:
"Virtual medical receptionist" describes three different products that happen to share a name: a remote human answering your calls, an AI voice agent, or a hybrid of the two. They do similar work. They do not cost similar money.


This guide works through what that gap actually buys, and the one question about these services that almost nobody asks.


## Key Takeaways


-


**The per-minute gap is enormous and verifiable.** Ruby's published plans work out at $3.45–$5.00 per minute. MedReception.ai's AI plans work out at 0.75–1.00. Retell AI publishes 0.07–0.31.


-


**Volume is what decides the model.** Below roughly 200 minutes a month, a human service is affordable and better at nuance. Above 1,000, the arithmetic becomes hard to argue with.


-


**Ask where your receptionist is physically sitting.** Several leading providers do not state it anywhere on their site. HIPAA obligations do not change with geography, but your practical leverage does.


-


**"Virtual" does not mean "cheap."** It means someone else manages the staffing. Whether that saves money depends entirely on which of the three models you buy.


## What a virtual medical receptionist actually is


A virtual medical receptionist answers your practice's calls from outside your building. It handles the front-desk work that does not require someone physically present: answering inbound calls, booking and rescheduling, taking messages, triaging to the right person, capturing new patient details and covering nights and weekends.


A quick disambiguation, because this phrase is genuinely overloaded. Search for it and you will find job boards alongside vendors. A large share of the people searching this term are looking for *work* as a remote receptionist, not for a service. This guide is for practices buying one.


### The three models


**Remote human receptionists.** Trained people, working from home or a contact centre, answering your line under your practice's name. Companies like MEDVA, WellReceived and Ruby operate this way. You are buying labour, managed by somebody else.


[AI voice agents](https://www.sully.ai/blog/ai-medical-receptionist) **.** Software that holds the conversation and takes the action: booking into your EHR, sending intake forms, routing urgent calls. No human on the line unless the system escalates.


**Hybrid.** AI takes the first pass and handles routine volume; humans take overflow, complex calls and anything the AI flags. Most serious deployments end up here eventually, whatever they started as.

Two things stand out.


**Human pricing barely improves with scale.** Ruby's cost per minute falls only from $5.00 to $3.45 as you move from the smallest plan to the largest, a 31% improvement across a tenfold increase in volume. That is what buying labour looks like: there is a floor, because someone has to be on the phone.


**AI pricing is nearly flat but starts an order of magnitude lower.** MedReception.ai moves from $0.99 to $0.75 per minute as volume grows. The saving is not in the discount curve; it is in the starting point.


For reference, an in-house receptionist earns a median **$38,010 a year, about $3,168 a month in salary alone** , before payroll tax or benefits, according to the[Bureau of Labor Statistics](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/office-and-administrative-support/receptionists.htm) . A human virtual service at 500 minutes a month costs roughly half that, with no employment obligations. An AI plan covering twice the minutes costs under a third.


### Where the published numbers stop


Be aware of what is not in those figures. Ruby states it charges no additional fees for activation, onboarding, setup or customisation. That is unusually clear, and worth having in writing from whoever you choose. But Ruby does not publish overage rates, and neither do most providers at the top end.


Most of the market publishes nothing at all. Of the[eight AI receptionist platforms we compared](https://www.sully.ai/blog/top-8-ai-medical-receptionists-in-2025) , only two published enough pricing to calculate a monthly bill. Among human services, MEDVA and WellReceived both route you to a sales conversation.


## The question almost nobody asks: where is your receptionist sitting?


This is the gap in every comparison of these services, and it matters more than most feature differences.


A remote human receptionist is a person, in a room, somewhere. That somewhere is frequently not the United States. Offshore staffing is a large part of how this model achieves its price. Yet on the pages we reviewed, **neither MEDVA nor WellReceived states where its receptionists are based.** MEDVA says its assistants are "HIPAA-trained, operating in monitored environments with strict security protocols." WellReceived says its team works "from their respective home offices." Neither names a country.


That is not an accusation of wrongdoing. HIPAA does not prohibit offshore business associates, and the obligations are identical wherever the work happens: any service handling PHI on your behalf is a business associate and requires a signed BAA before you disclose anything, as our[HIPAA guide](https://www.sully.ai/blog/hipaa-compliant-ai-receptionist) sets out and[per HHS](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/privacy/guidance/business-associates/index.html) .


What changes with geography is your practical position if something goes wrong. Your remedy is contractual, and contracts are easier to enforce against a company in your own jurisdiction. So ask, before signing:


-


**Where will people accessing our PHI physically be located?**


-


**Is any PHI stored or transmitted outside the United States?**


-


**If staff work from home offices, what controls apply there** (device management, screen recording, family members in the room)?


-


**Do our payer contracts restrict offshore handling of patient data?** Some do. Check before you sign, not after.


AI changes the shape of this question rather than removing it. There is no home office, but there is a chain of subcontractors (speech-to-text, language model, voice, carrier), and HHS requires a business associate to hold a BAA with each subcontractor before disclosing PHI to it. Either way, the honest question is the same: *who, specifically, hears my patients?*


## What human services still do better


The per-minute gap is not the whole argument, and it would be dishonest to pretend otherwise.


-


**Genuine judgement.** A distressed patient, an ambiguous situation, a request that does not fit the script. People handle exceptions; software escalates them.


-


**Empathy under pressure.** WellReceived claims 90% of patients prefer real people over AI and 71% say human agents show more empathy. Those are the company's own figures, unsourced, and plainly in its interest. Treat them as a vendor's position rather than evidence. But the underlying point is not controversial.


-


**Zero technical lift.** Forward your line and you are live. No EHR integration project, no conversation design, no escalation rules to configure.


-


**Low volume economics.** At 50–100 minutes a month, the absolute difference between $395 and $99 is not worth a project.


MEDVA states that most clients are matched with a receptionist within 48 hours, and claims 60% or more overhead cost reduction against in-house staff and 40% fewer voicemails within the first weeks. Those are the right metrics to ask any human provider to evidence for a practice like yours.


## What AI does better


-


**Volume without queueing.** A human service with 500 included minutes has a hard ceiling. AI handles concurrent calls, so three patients calling at once are all answered.


-


**Consistency.** It delivers prep instructions the same way at 2am as at 2pm, and never has an off day.


-


**Writing into the EHR.** The better AI platforms book directly into live availability. Most human services take a message for your staff to action, which moves work rather than removing it.


-


**Cost at scale.** Above roughly 1,000 minutes a month, the arithmetic stops being close.


## The hybrid model


Hybrid is where most practices end up: AI answers everything, handles the routine majority, and hands off anything clinical, emotional or ambiguous to a person. It is also the model that most reduces the risk of getting the decision wrong, because the failure mode is a transfer rather than a bad outcome.


OhMD, which sells in this category, publishes indicative ranges of 800–3,000 a month for remote human, 200–1,500 for AI-only and 300–1,200 for hybrid. Those are a competitor's estimates rather than a price list, but the ordering matches what the published per-minute figures show.


The thing to get right in a hybrid setup is the handoff. Ask how the human receives context when the AI transfers: do they get the transcript and the caller's details, or does the patient repeat everything? A hybrid that makes patients start again is worse than either model alone.

## The contract questions nobody asks


Pricing pages do not cover these, and they are where the surprises live.


1.


**What is the overage rate?** Most providers publish plan prices and not what happens when you exceed them. At human-service rates, overage is expensive.


2.


**What counts as a billable minute?** Does hold time count? Does a 20-second wrong number?


3.


**What is the minimum term, and the cancellation notice?** Annual lock-ins are common.


4.


**Who trains the receptionist on our practice, and what does it cost?** With human services this is real staff time, and it is yours.


5.


**What happens to our data when we leave?** Transcripts, recordings, call logs: can you export them, and will the vendor confirm deletion?


## Frequently Asked Questions


### How much does a virtual medical receptionist cost?


From published price lists: human services run 250–1,725 a month for 50–500 included minutes, which is 3.45–5.00 per minute. Managed AI plans run 495–1,495 for 500–2,000 minutes, roughly 0.75–1.00 per minute. Self-built AI runs 0.07–0.31 per minute. Many providers in both categories publish no pricing at all.


### What are the responsibilities of a virtual medical receptionist?


Answering and routing inbound calls, booking and rescheduling appointments, taking and relaying messages, capturing new patient intake details, verifying insurance information, sending reminders, and covering after-hours and overflow. What varies is whether they can write into your EHR or only take a message for staff to action.


### Is a virtual medical receptionist HIPAA compliant?


Only with a signed BAA covering the service. HHS requires satisfactory assurances in a written agreement before PHI is disclosed to any business associate, and that applies identically to a human service and an AI platform. Ask also about subcontractors, and about where staff are physically located.


### Is a human or an AI virtual receptionist better?


They fail differently, which is the useful way to think about it. Humans handle nuance and cost roughly five times more per minute. AI handles volume and consistency but needs well-designed escalation. Below 200 minutes a month, human; above 1,000, AI; in between, hybrid.


### Can a virtual receptionist book directly into our EHR?


Some can, many cannot. AI platforms increasingly write bookings into live availability; human services more often take a message for your staff. This single difference determines whether you have removed work or relocated it, so confirm it before signing.


### How much does a virtual medical receptionist make?


If you are searching as a job seeker rather than a practice: US receptionist roles have a median wage of $38,010 a year, or $18.27 an hour, per the Bureau of Labor Statistics, with remote medical reception roles varying widely by employer and scope. Employment across the occupation is projected to decline 2% between 2025 and 2035.


### Do we still need front-desk staff?


Almost always yes. Virtual reception covers the phone; it does not greet patients, handle in-person check-in, chase a provider down a corridor, or manage the waiting room. Practices typically redeploy front-desk time rather than remove the role.
